docs.title: Software Resilience and Reliability
docs.text:
Technology is the primary engine for value creation, innovation, and organizational performance. Unlike physical assets, software is not static. Its power lies in its ability to incorporate user feedback and evolve to meet changing needs. Consequently, one of the most critical indicators of a software application’s health is how easily, safely, and quickly it can be modified.

-- DORA / Google Cloud, 2026

docs.title: Target Audience and Technology Rationale
docs.text:
This book was written for new developers who have had some experience with programming, but may lack experience working in larger projects with larger codebases.

This book uses .NET and the C# programming language to illustrate concepts. These were chosen because:

  • The .NET runtime is cross-platform.
  • The language and platform afford the ability to demonstrate the concepts for this book.
  • The .NET ecosystem tends toward a "one right way to do it" philosophy than other more divergent technologies.

It is not expected that the reader have any C# experience. With the volume of high-quality, low-cost, accessible resources available at our disposible - it has never been easier to learn new programming languages and technologies.

This book uses application software as opposed to system software do demonstrate concepts. Application software is typically more accessible for new learners, and examples are easier to understand.

All of the topics in this book may be applied to software generally, regardless of which technology a solution is implemented in.

docs.title: Companion Code
docs.text:
All of the code for this book may be found within the Software Resilience and Reliability GitHub Organization. Chapters will reference any repositories that are used for code examples.

We encourage you to clone the repository and run the examples for yourself. The best way to learn software development concepts is to read, and try out, existing solutions.

You will need to install an IDE such as VS Code, as well as the .NET Software Development Kit and any additional extensions to support development in the C# language.

docs.title: Living Software
docs.text:
When describing a piece of software, we often use the word solution. Software primarily exists to solve problems that users are experiencing. These problems span a broad range of domains, or areas of application.

For example:

  • Our airline passengers need to browse flights and purchase tickets.
  • Our homeowners need to save energy by adjusting temperature when the house is empty.
  • Our retail suppliers need to forecast holiday demand and place inventory orders.
  • Our accountants need to enter spreadsheet data into the new accounting system.

Once a software solution is built, however, the problem isn't "solved". Software systems evolve to meet the changing needs of the users.

docs.title: Adding new features
docs.text: Software solves dynamic and complex problems. To meet the changing needs of users, new features are added and existing features are continuously improved.

docs.title: Removing low-value features
docs.text: Code is a liability because it must be maintained and it adds complexity to the codebase. Parts of an application that no longer add significant value should be removed.

docs.title: Fixing bugs
docs.text: Even the best systems have unexpected bugs that need to be fixed.

docs.title: Changing a technology implementation detail
docs.text:
Applications grow over time, and may need changes in hardware.

Third-party vendors (those providing software or hardward that don't directly work for your organization) may change terms, adjust prices, or go out of business.

Very often, technologies simply "age out". This may leave the system in a state where components are incompatible; part of the solution can no longer work well with another part.

docs.title: Removing technical debt
docs.text: Technical debt is the future costs associated with relying on shortcuts or suboptimal decisions made during software development. We will spend most of this book learning how to mitigate (prevent) and remediate (fix) techinical debt.

docs.title: Managing Complexity
docs.text: Arguably, the most difficult part of building software is managing complexity. For a given software problem there may be hundreds of ways to implement a solution. Dozens of these may be practical and effective. How do we know which to choose?

docs.title: Design Tradeoffs
docs.text:
In the world of software, there is no "best" solution. Each solution will involve tradeoffs. By understanding what is most important to our clients and the consumers of our software, we can adjust the development approaches that we take and get as close as possible.

As an example, when you were first learning to program you probably wrote mostly procedural code, with all of your code in one file.

You may later have learned some object oriented programming (OOP), where code is grouped into classes, usually with one file per class. OOP is not inherently better than procedural programming. It offers a tradeoff. There is a reason that small scripts are procedural whereas larger full scale applications tend to be object oriented:

Procedural

  • Quick initial development
  • Code "reads" sequentially so can be easier to understand
  • Difficult to maintain in large project
  • Poor modularity and code reuse

Object Oriented

  • Requires planning up front
  • Scattered files and extra "boilerplate code" can make it difficult ot understand
  • Isolated functionality makes maintence easy in large projects
  • Excellent modularity and code reuse

Right Tool for the Job

With the broad range of available options, simply choosing an appropriate technology can be a daunting task. It may be tempting to stick with a technology because you're familiar with it or because it's currently trendy. Some up front research into the pros and cons of each technology can help you make a more informed decision.

If all you need to do is read a CSV file and create a graph image from the contents, a procedural script written in a language like Python is a good choice.

If you need a full web application with complex user interactions and domain logic, object oriented programming written in a language like C# is a good choice.

docs.title: Costs Associated with Technical Debt
docs.text:
When comparing the two projects above, we could have also focused on other metrices like cost of change. We would see the inverse of the curves above: a project with well-managed technical debt will have low cost to change in later stages, while a project with poor technical debt management will have high cost to change.

These costs are often hidden, and don't manifest directly as measurable lost dollars for an organization.

docs.title: Fiscal cost
docs.text: The fiscal cost of a change is the direct monetary cost of the change. With software, this mostly means the cost of the labor to implement the change. Developers and other technical staff must be paid to fix issues.

docs.title: Opportunity cost
docs.text: Time spent fixing issues is time that is not spent on new features or improvements. This can lead to a backlog of work, which can lead to longer development cycles and lower productivity.

docs.title: Psychological cost
docs.text: Developers who spend most of their time fixing issues are more likely to be burnt out and unsatisfied with their work. This can lead to higher turnover and lower morale.

docs.title: Reputational cost
docs.text: Software providers with a reputation for rolling out software that is littered with bugs, or for being unable to deliver promised features on time, are more likely to lose customers.

docs.title: What is Technical Debt?
docs.text:
We previously defined technical debt as the future costs associated with relying on shortcuts or suboptimal decisions made during software development.

The idea aligns with the proverb "An ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure": adopting best practices early in the development process can prevent the need for costly fixes later.

Let's take a look at the image above.

On the x-axis is "time": the left side is early in the development process, the right side is late in the development process.

On the y-axis is "features delivered": early in the project there are no features. They are added over time.

The two curves represent two different projects:

Poor Technical Debt Management

The project in red does not manage technical debt well. This curve roughly has a logarithmic shape as the project progresses.

It may seem like quick progress early indicates that the project is off to a good start, but the reality is that the project is likely to fall behind later. It may even reach a point where nothing can be changed without breaking the system, and the project is effectively dead.

Well-Managed Technical Debt

The project in blue follows good practices for managing technical debt. This curve roughly has an exponential shape as the project progresses.
